context: podium & tower · residential/retail MEP segregation drives the fit-out and handover

brief.intro: A mixed-use residential project stacks a retail or commercial podium under one or more residential towers, so two very different buildings share one structure and one set of vertical services. The programme runs on two rhythms at once: a slow, complex podium and transfer structure at the base, and a fast, repetitive typical-floor cycle up the tower. Vertical services — power, water, fire fighting, data — must stay continuous through the transfer level even though retail and residential are metered, tested and handed over separately. Your schedule stands or falls on three things: getting the transfer structure right (it gates everything above it), keeping the typical-floor cycle running at a steady rhythm, and coordinating two independent fit-out and commissioning tracks that still share one life-safety system.

scope.name: Enabling & piling
scope.desc: Site clearance, piling and pile caps for the combined podium/tower foundation.

scope.name: Substructure & podium
scope.desc: Basement, podium slab and retail/parking levels below the tower.

scope.name: Transfer structure
scope.desc: Heavy transfer beams/slab carrying the tower's columns onto the wider podium grid — the geometric hinge between the two buildings.

scope.name: Retail podium shell & core
scope.desc: Retail floors, back-of-house and loading dock, typically handed over as landlord shell with shopfronts left to tenants.

scope.name: Residential tower superstructure
scope.desc: Core and typical-floor slab cycle repeated up the tower using jump/climbing form.

scope.name: Building envelope & façade
scope.desc: Curtain wall to the tower, cladding to the podium, roof and terrace waterproofing.

scope.name: Vertical MEP risers
scope.desc: Power, water, fire-fighting and data risers that must stay continuous through the transfer level.

scope.name: Vertical transportation
scope.desc: Passenger and service lifts, and escalators where present at the podium.

scope.name: Residential unit fit-out
scope.desc: First fix, wet-area waterproofing, tiling, second fix, joinery and snagging, repeated unit by unit.

scope.name: Testing, commissioning & phased handover
scope.desc: Life-safety systems tested as one integrated building, then residential and retail handed over on separate but coordinated dates.

must_get_right: The transfer structure is a hard gate — nothing above it, tower or podium, starts until it is cast, stressed and cured.
Keep vertical services continuous through the transfer/podium level — retail and residential risers cannot be designed or sequenced as if they were two separate buildings.
Protect the typical-floor cycle's rhythm — it is the tower's real productivity engine; any interruption echoes up every floor above it.
Plan two handovers, not one — retail shell-and-core and residential units follow different fit-out tracks but share one life-safety system that must be proven as a whole building first.

basis_of_planning.standard: AACE Recommended Practice 38R-06 — Documenting the Schedule Basis

sections.heading: Scheduling method & tools
sections.body: A Critical Path Method (CPM) network built in Primavera P6, developed to a Level 3 control schedule with retained-logic progress. The tower's typical-floor cycle is modelled as a repeating fragnet so productivity trends are visible floor-by-floor; the podium and transfer structure are modelled as discrete activities given their non-repetitive nature. Total float is kept ≥ 0 in the baseline.

sections.heading: Calendars & working time
sections.body: Substructure, podium and transfer-structure works run a 6-day week; the tower's typical-floor cycle runs on a fixed cycle-time calendar so trade gangs are resourced consistently; residential and retail fit-out move to two shifts where local regulations allow, to protect the handover date. A weather allowance is embedded in the façade-install calendar.

sections.heading: Sequencing logic & critical path
sections.body: The driving path runs piling → podium/transfer structure → tower core & typical-floor cycle → envelope close-out → vertical riser continuity through the podium → residential fit-out → integrated life-safety commissioning → phased handover. The transfer structure is a hard logic gate: no tower or podium activity above it can start until it is cast, stressed and cured. Retail fit-out is typically not critical once shell-and-core is handed over, but the integrated fire and life-safety test is, because it covers the whole building including retail.

sections.heading: Key assumptions
sections.body: Design is frozen and authority approvals obtained per phase gate; the transfer structure design and loading are finalised before tower design is frozen; a single mobilisation; retail tenants take shell-and-core handover on the published date without design changes flowing back into base-build. Any change to these invalidates the baseline dates.

sections.heading: Procurement & long-lead items
sections.body: The following are tracked as milestones and drive the network:

rows: Before shaft close-out on affected floors

sections.heading: Access, resource & site constraints
sections.body: Tower crane and hoist capacity is the binding constraint on the typical-floor cycle — jump-form, façade panels, MEP risers and finishing materials all compete for the same lift; a materials-hoist and logistics plan is part of the baseline, not an afterthought. Podium and tower fronts often share one site access and laydown area, so retail and residential trades must be sequenced to avoid congestion at the base.

sections.heading: Risks, float & contingency
sections.body: Principal risks: transfer-structure design or construction delay (it gates everything above), façade lead-time slippage stalling weather-tightness, and a failed integrated life-safety test forcing a re-test across the whole building. Schedule contingency is held after transfer-structure completion and before the integrated commissioning test, rather than spread thinly across the typical-floor cycle.

sections.heading: Schedule levels of detail
sections.body: Reported at Level 1 (milestones) and Level 2 (summary) to the client; controlled at Level 3, with the tower typical-floor cycle tracked as a repeating fragnet; expanded to Level 4–5 lookahead for the field — consistent with AACE 37R-06.
